text: 1 Consent by Dr/ Somaya Madkour Professor of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology Alexandria University 2 Consent ILO’s. 1. Differentiate types of consents in the medical field. 2. Apply the principals of informed consent and how to be valid and documented. 3. Differentiate the exceptions to require a consent. 4. Respect the patient’s right to refuse treatment. Consent is a central topic in bioethics. It lies at the heart of the relationship between the patient and the health care professional. The patient relies on the professional’s expertise, knowledge and advice, but it is up to the patient to decide whether he/she will accept or reject treatment, or in some circumstances request that the professional make the decision. What does consent mean?? a) Consent is the giving of permission or agreement for an intervention (whether diagnostic or therapeutic) following a process of communication about the proposed intervention. b) Consent must be obtained before starting treatment or investigations, or providing personal or social care for a patient or involving a patient in teaching and research. c) All patients have the right to be involved in decisions about their treatment and care and to make informed decisions if they can. d) The exchange of information between doctor and patient is essential to good decision making. serious harm can result if patients are not listened to, or if they are not given the information they need - and time and support to understand it - so they can make informed decisions about their care. Obtaining valid consent is an ethical obligation and legal compulsion • Informed consent is essential to ethics, which upholds the principles of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice: • Treating a patient without informed consent could result in legal action for assault against the Health Practitioner who provided the care, irrespective of whether the patient suffered harm as a result of the procedure (constitutes medical malpractice). Consent in medical practice is needed in the following situations: 1-Examination of a patient for the purpose of diagnosis and subsequent treatment. 2- Examination of a patient for medico-legal purposes. 3- Involving patients in medical research studies. Why is consent important? • To protect the patient from unauthorized procedures. • To protect the physician from claims of malpractice. If the consent is not obtained, the patient has the right to sue for medical malpractice Types of consent: 1- Implied consent (Known by the behavior of the patient) • The act of a patient entering a doctor's chamber and expressing his problem is taken as an implied consent for general physical examination (patient has consented to abdominal 3 palpation when voluntarily undressing and lying on couch) and routine investigations such as X-rays etc… • When he/she offers an arm for venipuncture (giving a blood sample). • The act of the patient standing in line to receive a vaccination. • Express (oral or written) consent It means that the Patient expressly asks the doctor to provide care and consents by direct words, oral or written. This consent should be obtained for any procedure that carries any risk, and therefore, patient-specific agreement must be obtained before the procedure starts. • The patient or his/her representative has the right to be provided with sufficient information by the physician to allow him/her to make an informed decision to decide whether or not to consent to a certain procedure. Oral consent is valid, but it is usual to obtain written consent for major procedures. a) Oral consent: ▪ For intimate examinations e.g., vaginal and rectal. ▪ Simple procedures e.g., insertion of an intravenous cannula. ▪ Procedures performed under local anesthesia e.g., suture of minor lacerations. b) Written consent: For more invasive tests or for major procedures with significant risks e.g. ▪ blood transfusion ▪ breast biopsy ▪ all operations requiring general or spinal anesthesia. What are the requirements for obtaining a valid consent? 1) the patient giving consent must have capacity 2) the consent must be freely given 3) the consent must be sufficiently specific to the procedure or treatment proposed 4) the consent must be informed. The four criteria for a valid consent must be met irrespective of whether the consent is in writing or oral. 1) Capacity The patient must have the capacity to give consent. A person has decision making capacity if they can: • understand the facts and choices involved • weigh up the consequences and evaluate the personal cost and benefit of each of the consequences and relate them to your own set of values and priorities • communicate their decision. Legally, adults are presumed to have capacity to consent to or refuse medical treatment unless otherwise indicated. A person is incapable of giving consent to the carrying out of medical treatment if the person: (a) is incapable of understanding the general nature and effect of the proposed treatment, or (b) is incapable of indicating whether or not he or she consents or does not consent to the treatment being carried out General principles to follow when assessing capacity: • always presume a person has capacity 4 • capacity is decision-specific (for example capacity may fluctuate or certain simple health treatments may be within a person’s capacity to consent whilst others may not) • respect a person’s privacy • substitute decision making is a last resort 2) Freely given: Consent must be freely given. The patient must not be pressured, coerced or intimidated into giving consent by Health Service staff, a Health Practitioner, a carer or a family member. 3) Sufficiently specific: The consent must be specific and is valid only for the condition being treated and the specified treatment or procedure about which the patient has been informed and agreed to. 4) Informed: The patient must be informed in broad terms of the nature and purpose in a way that the patient can understand. Health Practitioners have a duty to provide the patient with enough information to enable them to gain an understanding of the nature and effects of the operation, procedure or treatment, the risks associated with it and any alternatives to the proposed treatment. • So consent must be given voluntary by an appropriately informed patient who has the capacity to consent to the proposed procedure (the patient or his guardian as in case of minor responsible about them) • If the patient does not know what the intervention entails …. it is not consent • If patients are not able to do all of the components, family members, court- appointed guardians, or others (as determined by law) may act as "surrogate decision-makers" and make decisions for you. • A valid Consent is not given for illegal act as criminal abortion and euthanasia. Sometimes ethical beliefs and legal rights do not always coincide. We cannot legally consent to voluntary euthanasia, since it is illegal, even if we feel strongly that it should be permitted. • A valid Informed Consent should be obtained by a health care provider who is involved with the patient's care. The seven principles of decision making and consent Every physician should be familiar with this document (GMC guidelines) 1) All patients have the right to be involved in decisions about their treatment and care and be supported to make informed decisions if they are able. 2) Decision making is an ongoing process focused on meaningful dialogue: ( it is not one way thing , it is 2 way and sometimes family member , friends may be involved ) the exchange of relevant information specific to the individual patient. 3) All patients have the right to be listened to, and to be given the information they need to make a decision and the time and support they need to understand it. 4) Doctors must try to find out what matters to patients so they can share relevant information about the benefits and harms of proposed options and reasonable alte

name: PDF: intra-interprof
text: 1 Interprofessional & Intraprofessional Relationships in Healthcare By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Define Interprofessional and Intraprofessional Relationships 2. Identify competencies of intra/ interprofessional collaboration 3. Demonstrate effective communication Strategies for collaborating with other healthcare professionals. 4. Discuss Common Barriers to effective professional communication 5. Explain Intra/Interprofessional significance in healthcare settings. 6. Analyze Ethical Issues in Interprofessional Relationships Definitions: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), interprofessional collaboration occurs when “multiple health workers from different professional backgrounds work together with patients, families, caregivers and communities to deliver the highest quality of care across settings.” E.g. collaboration between physicians, nurses, pharmacists, physical therapists and the social care profession. Regarding the intraprofessional relationship, it is the collaboration between two or more disciplines within the same profession e.g. collaboration between a pediatrician and neurosurgeon for the sake of the patient. Competencies of intra/ interprofessional collaboration: Competencies identified for intra/interprofessional collaboration are categorized into six domains: 1. Patient-centered care 2. Interprofessional communication 3. Participatory leadership 4. Conflict resolution 5. Transparency of duties and responsibilities 6. Teamwork 2 1. Patient-centered care: Patient-centered care is one of the main competencies in the healthcare system. It ensures the safety and quality of healthcare. Patient-centered care is the degree to which patients and their families are satisfied with their care and involved in decision making process and to which those providing the care do so with sensitivity and respect for the patient’s need, expectations and individual differences. One of the dimensions of patient-centered care is the coordination and smooth transition from one healthcare setting to another. 2. Intra/ interprofessional communication: It describes the sharing of information (by means of verbal, writing or other medium) among members of different health professionals’ fields in a responsive and responsible manner that supports a team and influence patient care positively. Components of Intra/ Interprofessional Communication • Effective communication tools, information systems and communication technologies that facilitate interactions. • Avoiding discipline-specific terminology when communicating information with patients, families, community members. • Expressing one’s knowledge and opinions to team members with clarity, and respect to ensure common understanding of information. • Active listening to encourage ideas and opinions of other team members. • Giving sensitive, constructive feedback to others about their performance on the team. • Using respectful language in difficult situations, or during conflict. General Barriers to Intra/ Interprofessional Communication: • Personal values and expectations and personality differences • Organizational hierarchy • Varying team members who may not have worked together before • Cultural diversity and generational differences • Historical interprofessional and intraprofessional competitions 3 • Differences in language and medical jargon • Differences in schedules and professional routines • Varying levels of preparation, qualifications, and status • Fears of diluted professional identity • Diverse clinical responsibilities • Increased complexity of patient care • Emphasis on rapid decision-making ISBARR communication model: A common format used by health care team members to exchange client information is ISBARR, a mnemonic for the components of Introduction, Situation, Background, Assessment, Request/Recommendations, and Repeat back. • Introduction: Introduce your name, role, and the agency from which you are calling. • Situation: Provide the patient’s name and location, the reason you are calling, recent vital signs, and the status of the patient. • Background: Provide background information about the patient such as admission date and diagnosis, current condition , recent relevant lab or diagnostic results, previous illnesses and allergies. • Assessment: Share abnormal assessment findings and your evaluation of the current situation. • Request/Recommendations: such as reassessment, order a lab/diagnostic test, prescribe/change medication. • Repeat back: to confirm accuracy. Be sure to document communication in the patient’s chart. 3. Participatory leadership: It is a unique leadership style, also referred to as democratic leadership. Participative leaders recognize the significant role of all members in team success, so they encourage all team members to provide feedback and participate in shared decision-making. They also promote transparent communication and collaborative solutions. 4 4. Conflict resolution: It happens when healthcare providers work as a team that actively engages in addressing disagreements and responding effectively to all types of conflict . To support interprofessional practice, health providers should: • create a safe environment where differing opinions are welcome • validate and acknowledge differing perspectives • communicate positively and constructively • see conflict with the potential for a positive outcome 5. Teamwork: A multidisciplinary team is a group of individuals from different professional backgrounds, each bringing their own specialized expertise to work together on a common goal which is achieving patient-centered care. 6. Transparency of duties and responsibilities: This competence helps all team members to understand their own and others' roles and duties and use one another's knowledge and skills to perform the right task. Significance of Inter/Intra professional relation in healthcare settings: Both are increasingly recognized as important due to the complex and dynamic nature of healthcare organizations and the growing specialization of healthcare professions. They are essential to: 1. Enhances patient care and outcomes When healthcare professionals work together, they can provide comprehensive and well-coordinated care by ensuring that all aspects of a patient’s condition are addressed, leading to more accurate diagnoses and treatment plans. 2. Mitigates medical errors According to the Joint Commission, miscommunication during patient handoffs contributes to an estimated 80% of serious medical errors. By working together, 5 healthcare providers can identify and address potential safety issues more effectively regarding medication management, patient handoffs, and care transitions, which are critical points for errors. 3. Expedites initiation of treatment A substantial proportion of healthcare is marked by waiting periods. Patients await physician consultations and physicians await input from other interprofessional team members. Communication delays allow medical conditions to deteriorate. A clinical collaboration platform efficiently delivers pertinent information to the right individuals at the right time via secure messaging, voice, or video leading to a better quality of care. 4. Diminishes inefficiencies and healthcare costs Interprofessional collaboration ensures more efficient resource utilization, leading to cost savings and improved resource allocation. For example, when a team of professionals collaborates on a patient’s care plan, unnecessary tests and procedures and duplicated work can be avoided, reducing both the financial burden on patients and the strain on healthcare facilities. 5. Advances staff relations and job satisfaction Optimizing clinical workflows through improved interdisciplinary collaboration helps reduce burnout and improve clinician satisfaction. On the contrary, poor intra- and interprofessional teamwork is associated with higher rates of inadequate or missed care, medical errors

Misunderstanding in interpreting the principle of beneficence by not understanding the patient’s likely desires. Failing to avoid harm (non-maleficence) through creating suffering, both in the patient, the relatives. Dr. Smith, a junior doctor in the emergency department, needs to communicate the status of a patient, Mr. Doe, to Dr. Brown, the on-call surgeon. Mr. Doe, a 67-year-old male with a history of diabetes and hypertension, was admitted to the ED with severe abdominal pain. After initial assessment and investigations, Dr. Smith suspects acute cholecystitis. Dr. Smith followed ISBAR Communication: Which of the following details is part of the 'Background' in ISBAR? A. Mr. Doe's vitals B. Mr. Doe's history of diabetes and hypertension C. The recommendation for surgical assessment D. The suspected diagnosis of acute cholecystitis B Why is the ISBAR model important in interprofessional communication? A. It ensures that only the most senior staff communicate with each other. B. It provides a structured way to communicate critical information. C. It allows for informal and flexible communication styles. D. It is used only for non-urgent cases. B Dr. Jones, a family physician, and Nurse Brown work together in a community clinic. They have a new patient, Mrs. Smith, a 45-year-old woman with a recent diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes. Mrs. Smith is anxious about managing her condition and requires a comprehensive care plan involving lifestyle changes and medication management. Dr. Jones and Nurse Brown need to collaborate effectively to provide holistic care. Additionally, within the clinic, Dr. Jones also needs to work with Dr. Lee, another family physician, to ensure continuity of care for patients when one of them is unavailable. Which of the following best describes intraprofessional collaboration in this case? A. Dr. Jones working with Nurse Brown B. Nurse Brown working in community clinic C. Dr. Jones and Dr. Lee coordinating patient care within the same clinic D. Nurse Brown referring Mrs. Smith to a dietitian C Why is it important for Dr. Jones and Dr. Lee to coordinate care for their patients within the clinic? A. To avoid duplication of services and ensure continuity of care B. To limit patient interactions with multiple physicians C. To establish a competitive environment within the clinic D. To ensure that one physician has complete control over patient care A Physician responsibilities towards community 1. Describe the key responsibilities of physicians towards their communities. 2. Explain the importance of public health and preventive medicine. 3. Discuss the ethical obligations to engage in disaster management. 4. Identify physician’s role in response to violence and abuse. 5. Define the E. professionalism. 6. Discuss ethical conduct when sharing medical content on media. 7. Define competency and explain how a physician could fulfill it. Physicians' primary ethical obligation to individual patients is to diagnose and treat illnesses through using their expertise, ensure patients receive the best possible care plus educate patients about their conditions and treatments to make informed decisions about their health. However, they also have a responsibility towards the whole community. They participate in activities to protect and promote the health of the public and to protect public safety. Key responsibilities of physicians towards their communities 1. Public Health and Preventive Medicine: Public health focuses on protecting and improving the health of populations through: Education, Policymaking, Screening and Researching for disease and injury prevention. 1. Public Health and Preventive Medicine: a. Preventive Care: Be updated about preventive care guidelines that are well supported by the best available evidence. Recommend and encourage patients to have appropriate vaccinations and screenings. b. Screening and reporting infectious diseases: Support routine, universal screening for infectious diseases as HBV, HCV, HIV. Respect for autonomy / a patient’s informed decision to make the test or not. Test patients without prior consent only in limited cases. Ensure that patients who tested + ve receive appropriate care. Report the specific authority and notify the endangered 3rd party. Safeguard the confidentiality of patient to the possible extent when reporting. 1. Public Health and Preventive Medicine: 1. Public Health and Preventive Medicine: c. Injury prevention from impaired drivers: Assess at-risk patients for conditions adversely affect their driving ability. If physicians are not able to evaluate the effect of medical condition, refer patient for assessment Help the patient through options for treatment if available. Prior to reporting, explain to the patient that you have an obligation to report a medically at-risk driver as continuing to drive poses a clear risk to public safety. d. Routine universal immunization of physicians: Physicians have an ethical responsibility to encourage patients to accept immunization. They also have to take appropriate measures in their own practice to prevent the spread of infectious disease in health care settings. Regarding highly transmissible diseases, that pose significant medical risk for vulnerable patients, and for which there is an available, safe, and effective vaccine, physicians have a responsibility to accept immunization if there is no contraindication. 1. Public Health and Preventive Medicine: Participate in public health campaigns, workshops or seminars to raise awareness about important health issues such as smoking cessation, nutrition, and mental health. Educate patients about relevant modifiable risk factors. Promote training in health promotion during medical school. Support research to improve the evidence for health promotion. 2. Health promotion and education: 3. Physicians’ Responsibilities in Disaster Response & Preparedness: Maintaining the patients’ interests. Treating patients with equal respect, compassion and dignity. Respecting patient autonomy, privacy and confidentiality as possible. Treating patients’ family members with respect as they also need support. Advocating for accountability, fairness, equity and justice in the provision of health care and the allocation of health care resources. Advocating for accountability, fairness, equity and justice in the treatment of the health care workforce and the safety of the health care environment. Working collaboratively and supporting colleagues and other health care professionals during and after a disaster. Looking after one’s own health and well-being in order to be able to care for others. Physicians have an ethical obligation to take appropriate action to avert the harm caused by violence and abuse. Physicians should be familiar with: How to detect and response to violence or abuse. Community and health resources that are available to abused persons. Public health measures that are effective in preventing violence and abuse. Legal requirements for reporting violence or abuse. 4. Identifying, treating and reporting violence & Abuse: Raise public awareness about the abuse, violence, DV. Consider abuse as a possible factor in the medical complaints. Identify signs of abuse to reduce the unidentified cases. Treat the immediate symptoms and sequelae of violence. Provide ongoing care to address long-term consequences of violence. Discuss any suspicion of abuse sensitively with the patient. Report suspected violence after informing patients. Protect patient privacy by disclosing only the minimum necessary information. 4. Identifying, treating and reporting violence & Abuse: In addition, physicians should not be influenced by misconceptions about abuse, including beliefs that it is rare, does not occur in “normal” families, and is a private matter best resolved without outside interference, or is caused by victims’ own actions. 5. Reporting of Adverse Events Post marketing, cases in which there is a causal relationship between use of a drug and an adverse event, especially a serious event, may be rare. A physician who suspects that an adverse reaction to a drug or medical device has occurred, whatever its severity, has an ethical responsibility to manage these adverse events and to communicate that information to the professional community through established reporting mechanisms. Physicians involved in the media environment should be aware of their ethical obligations to patients, the public, and the medical profession; and that their conduct can affect their medical colleagues, other health care professionals, as well as institutions with which they are affiliated. Media includes both the traditional media (radio and TV) and the new social media platforms. E-Professionalism is the professional use of electronic platforms. It includes online attitudes, actions, and adherence to relevant professional codes of conduct and principles including honesty, integrity, reliability, responsibility, and respect. 6. E-professionalism and ethical conduct in the media: 6. E-professionalism and ethical conduct in the media: Physicians should: Always remember that they are physicians first and foremost, and must uphold the values, norms, and integrity of the medical profession. Know that sharing information would threaten public health due to the spread of false perceptions and opinions. Reveal their identity (name and qualification) when sharing medical content. It is not acceptable to make an anonymous profile and share medical content with the public through it. You are completely responsible for your shared content. Never to disclose patient’s information on media. 6. E-professionalism and ethical conduct in the media: Aware that any information they share on media, may be disseminated to a larger audience and are difficult to remove as other users may distribute it further or comment on it. So, the shared information should be: Truthful and accurate. Concise. Up to date. Easy for patients to understand. Clear from any uncertain content that could be taken out of the situation. Supported with medical peer-reviewed literature. General medical advice with encouraging audience members to seek out qualified physicians to address their unique concerns. Conflict of interest must be revealed especially when sharing about any services or products. 7. Physician Competence, Self-Assessment & Self-Awareness: Competency refers to having the knowledge and skills necessary to perform the job effectively, which comes from training and experience. Physicians at all stages of their professional lives need to be able to recognize when they are and when they are not able to provide appropriate care for patients. CME about recent medical technology and advancements. Cultivate continuous self-awareness and self-observation. Seek feedback from peers and others. Maintain their own health and wellness. Be attentive to environmental and other factors that may compromise their ability to bring appropriate skills to the care of individual patients and act in the patient’s best interest. Dr. Taylor, a young and tech-savvy physician, frequently uses social media to share updates about medical advancements and engage with both colleagues and the public. Recently, Dr. Taylor posted a photo of himself and his team in the clinic, which unintentionally included a patient's medical chart visible in the background. A colleague noticed this and privately messaged Dr. Taylor, pointing out the potential breach of patient confidentiality. Dr. Taylor quickly deleted the post and issued an apology, but the incident had already been seen by several followers. What principle of e-professionalism was violated in this scenario? A. Maintaining a professional image B. Avoiding interactions with patients on social media C. Ensuring patient confidentiality and privacy D. Using proper medical terminology C Dr. Williams, a primary care physician, is seeing Ms. Laura, a 30-year-old woman, for a routine check-up. During the examination, Dr. Williams notices several bruises on Ms. Laura's arms and back. When asked about the bruises, Ms. Laura hesitates and then states that she fell down the stairs. Dr. Williams suspects that Ms. Laura may be a victim of domestic violence. What is Dr. Williams' primary ethical obligation in this scenario? To maintain patient confidentiality above all else To discuss the concerns and mandatory reporting with Ms. Laura To ignore the suspicions as Ms. Laura fell down the stairs To focus on treating the physical injuries of Ms. Laura B

text: Values, Beliefs , and Facts Ahmed A Elsheshai MD, MRCPsych psychiatrist Medical procedures for personal values Patients may ask for procedures for their own personal values and beliefs Aesthetic procedures Circumcision Preventive surgery In this case Make sure it is for the best interest of the patient Keep in mind their own religious and social background Take great care with your consent process Children  parents or court Refusal of treatment You must respect a competent patient’s decision to refuse an investigation or treatment, even if you think their decision is wrong or irrational. Children whose parents refuse treatment on religious or cultural background discuss their concerns and look for treatment options that will accommodate their beliefs. Involve the child in a way appropriate to their age and maturity If treatment is life saving and no other option is available, you should approach the court Conscientious objection You may choose to opt out of providing a particular procedure because of your personal beliefs and values, as long as this does not result in direct or indirect discrimination against, or harassment of, individual patients or groups of patients. This means you must not refuse to treat a particular patient or group of patients because of your personal beliefs or views about them. And you must not refuse to treat the health consequences of lifestyle choices to which you object because of your beliefs Discussion of beliefs & Self disclosure You should ask about beliefs and values and try to understand and empathize with the patient wherever possible In doing so you should not ask a patient to justify or discuss these beliefs Example: diabetic patients fasting Ramadan You may talk about your own personal beliefs only if the patient asks or directly indicates that they would welcome such input. In doing so you should only state your beliefs and values without imposition on the patient or causing them distress. Example: stage III cancer patient refuses treatment because they welcome death Example 1 A doctor refuses to perform hepatic transplant to a chronic alcohol user, because: He believes the patient brought this on himself The patient’s blood alcohol level indicates recent intoxication The patient is old and there are younger patients who need this liver The patient’s general condition does not support the major operation Example 2 A doctor treats AIDS but refrains from treating a patient who is promiscuous or homosexual because They increased their chances of contracting the illness by making certain lifestyle choices. They brought this on themselves (divine punishment). According to the ethical construct of justice, treatment and resources should be reserved for people with lower chance of reinfection. According to the doctor’s personal beliefs he chooses to refrain from treating this particular individual. Example 3 A doctor insists that his obese patient must lose weight before he will prescribe any medication, because: He believes the medication will be ineffective (futile) due to morbid obesity The doctor does not believe in intermediary solutions and pain-killers He intends to corner the patient into doing the right thing by denying him pain killers The doctor himself was obese and believes the patient can lose weight as he did Example 4 A plastic surgeon demands psychiatric evaluation to a patient who is requesting rhinoplasty, because: People should not change the way God made them She is from a moderate socio-economic class and there must be better things to spend her money on. He thinks she really looks pretty and that there is no need for any modification He fears that her request may reflect a defect in self-esteem resulting from depression or body dysmorphic disorder Case An 8-week pregnant woman has been exposed to radiation. She was told by her obstetrician that there is a considerable chance that the child has been deformed. There may be grounds for abortion, but the doctor prefers to wait and see if the child really has deformities. The mother is apprehensive and choses to go with abortion anyway because: “why take a risk when I can skip this pregnancy and bear another child”. Outline the values and beliefs of the patient and the doctor. Reflect on the doctor’s choices and what is the best course of action References Sagiv L, Roccas S, Cieciuch J, Schwartz SH. Personal values in human life . Nature Human Behaviour . 2017 Sep;1(9):630 schwarz theory of values Beck JS. Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond. Guilford press; 2011 Jason Giesbrecht. Personal Values and Beliefs Course slides. Plus2019 https://www.gmc-uk.org/-/media/documents/personal-beliefs-and-medical-practice-20200217_pdf-58833376.pdf LOs Differentiate the terms “value” and “belief” Enumerate basic values and identify examples for each List sources of beliefs and identify examples for each Assess their own value and belief systems Correlate the impact of values and beliefs on patient care Solve ethical vignettes related to value and belief conflict. Thank you Value Broad desirable goals that motivate people’s actions and serve as guiding principles in their lives (1) Schwarz theory of basic values (2) Universalism Benevolence Conformity/tradition Security Power Achievement Hedonism Stimulation Self direction Belief Core beliefs are defined as fundamental, inflexible, absolute, and generalised beliefs that people hold about themselves, others, the world, and/or the future (3) Activity Divide into 4 groups. Each group will try to come up with as many values and beliefs about one topic. Smoking Alcohol use Doctors’ immigration Body image Sports Doctors’ personal beliefs Doctors may practice medicine in accordance with their beliefs, provided that they act in accordance with relevant legislation and: do not treat patients unfairly do not deny patients access to appropriate medical treatment or services do not cause patients distress. Patient’s values vs doctor’s values
